analysis.one_liner: Makes mortgage servicers pay triple damages and daily fines when they botch escrow payments.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, vote, or cosponsor and died in the House Financial Services Committee when the Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: When homeowners pay their mortgage, servicers often hold money in an escrow account to pay property taxes and homeowners insurance on the homeowner's behalf. This bill would have amended a 1974 law so that when a servicer fails to make those payments on time, the homeowner can recover triple the actual damages in court, and the servicer owes the federal government a $1,000 fine for every day a homeowner goes without insurance coverage because of the failure. The fines collected would fund down-payment help for low-income families and legal advocacy groups that defend consumer rights.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners with federally related mortgages whose servicers hold escrow money for taxes and insurance. Under current law they can recover only actual damages for escrow failures; this bill would have tripled that and created a daily federal penalty when a servicer's mistake causes an insurance lapse, which can leave a family unprotected against fire, storm, or liability and trigger force-placed insurance bills.

how_it_helps.text: Borrowers in individual or class actions could recover three times their actual damages when a servicer fails to make timely escrow payments for insurance, taxes, or other charges [S2][S3].
Servicers would owe the Secretary a $1,000 civil penalty for each full or partial day of insurance coverage lapse caused by a missed escrow payment [S2][S3].
90% of the fines would fund down-payment assistance for low-income families buying a principal residence, and 10% would fund nonprofits doing consumer-rights legal advocacy [S3][S2].

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage loan servicers, who would face triple damages in borrower lawsuits and per-day federal fines for escrow failures. Some of that cost would likely be passed on to borrowers through servicing fees.

drawbacks.text: The bill text applies treble damages and penalties to servicer escrow failures without adding a safe harbor for good-faith errors or payment disputes, which could raise servicing costs that get passed to all borrowers through higher fees [S3].
The use of collected fines depends on annual appropriation Acts, so the promised down-payment and consumer-advocacy funding would only flow if Congress chose to appropriate it [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a real, documented harm: servicers that collect homeowners' escrow money but fail to pay taxes or insurance on time, leaving families uninsured or facing tax penalties. Its remedies (treble damages plus a per-day fine) are strong but aimed at a narrow set of failures, and the main cost would fall on the servicing industry, partly passed through to borrowers. It was a modest, focused bill rather than a sweeping overhaul.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the House Financial Services Committee, and then to a housing subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no vote, and not a single cosponsor until the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Andrews introduced the bill on July 27, 2005, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services [S1][S5].
On September 19, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Housing and Community Opportunity, and the action record shows no further steps [S5].
The bill attracted zero cosponsors [S4] and never received a committee markup or floor vote before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage servicers, who avoided new liability for escrow failures, and no homeowner gained the added protections, since the bill never advanced past committee.

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Andrews
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and pursued no visible further action as it stalled in committee; no other member joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over mortgage servicing law
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction, sent it to its housing subcommittee, and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill died there.

sides.party_line_note: With a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors, and no votes ever taken, the record shows no pattern of party support or opposition — the bill simply never moved.

industries.note: Servicers collect homeowners' escrow money and are supposed to pay taxes and insurance on time; the bill would have exposed them to treble damages and $1,000-per-day fines when they fail. Their interest in weaker escrow enforcement runs directly against homeowners who bear the harm of lapsed coverage and unpaid taxes.

The bill would have directed 10% of collected fines to nonprofits doing consumer-rights legal advocacy, giving such groups a new funding stream if the law took effect and Congress appropriated the money.
